tour.title: South Delhi: Sultans, Saints and Tombs
tour.summary: Eight centuries of Delhi in one walk: Sufi tombs, a stepwell, the great minar and a lakeside madrasa, with one honest metro hop.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to south Delhi, where eight centuries of sultans, saints and tomb-builders are stacked so tightly you can walk between dynasties before lunch.

Delhi has been sacked, rebuilt and renamed at least seven times — each new city layered on the last one's rubble — and it is still doing it. This is the capital of the world's largest democracy and a metro of more than thirty million people, where Mughal tombs sit next to metro stations and Sufi shrines draw Hindu and Muslim devotees alike. That easy mixing is real, and so is the tension underneath it: the same stones get claimed by different histories, sometimes loudly. You will see both the sharing and the scars today, starting with a mosque built from twenty-seven demolished temples. Hold both facts at once. Delhi does.

This tour runs in three acts, and each one has a different century in charge. Act one is Mehrauli Archaeological Park: a Sufi poet's tiled tomb, the rubble of Delhi's most feared thirteenth-century sultan, a four-storey stepwell you can climb down, and a Mughal tomb a British Resident once stole as a party house. Act two is the Qutub Complex, the walled garden where it all started: the tallest brick minaret on earth, India's first mosque built from twenty-seven temples' worth of carved stone, a sixteen-hundred-year-old pillar that refuses to rust, and the first true dome ever raised in India. Act three, after a short metro ride, is Hauz Khas: a fourteenth-century lakeside university with royal tombs on the terrace and a deer park on the shore.

One honest logistical note, because the voice in your ear refuses to lie to you. Mehrauli Park to the Qutub Complex is a genuine stroll, about two and a half kilometres through lanes and park trails. But the Qutub Complex to Hauz Khas is five kilometres of Delhi traffic — about seventy minutes on foot — and no honest guide would call that a stroll. So this tour does what Delhiites do: it takes the Yellow Line. Four stops on the metro, about forty minutes door to door, and the directions at Alai Darwaza spell out exactly how. Walked end to end it is eight kilometres and just under two hours on foot, mostly flat, with steps at the stepwell and uneven ground in the park.

Two house rules. Rule one: only the Qutub Complex charges entry, with separate Indian and foreign prices, and every rupee figure I quote is a snapshot, so verify at the gate and never blame the nice voice. Rule two: Delhi's heat is the real antagonist of this walk. Go in October to March if you can, start at opening time whatever the month, carry water, and let the baoli and the lake do their ancient cooling work. Your feet, like the sultans' architects, will thank you for planning.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. About 2.2 km of mostly flat walking plus one metro ride; uneven earth paths in Mehrauli Park, steep unrailed steps at the stepwell, and a few steps at most monuments.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at opening time, around 07:30 to 08:00, from October to March when Delhi is at its kindest. Avoid midday from April to June; if you must go in summer, do Mehrauli at dawn, rest through noon, and take Hauz Khas for sunset.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Jamali Kamali Mosque and Tomb
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open-access ASI monument inside Mehrauli Archaeological Park. No ticket and no gate; verify locally as ASI rules change.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily, roughly sunrise to sunset. Best in daylight; the park lanes are unlit after dark.
stops.accessibility: Uneven earth and stone paths through the park. Steps up into the mosque courtyard; not step free.
stops.insiderTip: Step inside the tomb chamber and look at the tiled ceiling: the verses are inlaid in enamelled faience, some of the finest tilework the Mughals ever set in stone.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the lane you came in on and turn right along the main park trail heading roughly north east for about 200 metres. The low ruined walls on your right are the tomb of a sultan.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Harvinder Chandigarh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Start with a love story, because Delhi does those unusually well. Jamali was the pen name of Sheikh Fazlullah, a celebrated Sufi poet who travelled widely in the early 1500s and ended up a favourite at the courts of Sikandar Lodi and Babur. Kamali is believed to have been his close companion, and the two men were buried side by side in this chamber in 1528 and 1536. The mosque beside it went up around the same time, and the whole ensemble is one of the last great works of the Lodi age, finished just as the Mughals arrived to change everything.

Walk into the mosque courtyard first. The prayer hall is faced in red sandstone with five arches, and the central bay carries some of the most delicate ornament in Delhi: medallions, calligraphy and tile inlay in blue, green and turquoise. This is the moment Lodi architecture learned to show off, right before the empire that built it disappeared.

Then step into the tomb chamber next door. It is a square room with a flat-ish dome, and the ceiling is the reason you came: verses and patterns in enamelled faience tile, deep blue and turquoise against the plaster. Look for the grave of Jamali himself, inscribed with his own Persian couplet boasting that his tomb would outlast the world. Arrogant? Perhaps. But nearly five hundred years later, you are standing in it, reading his words, so the man had a point.

One piece of atmosphere before you leave. The Archaeological Survey gardens around you hold half a dozen more anonymous Lodi tombs, and on Thursday evenings qawwali singers sometimes gather near the dargah. If you hear harmonium music drifting over the walls, follow it: this complex has been a place of poetry and pilgrimage for five centuries, and it still is.

stops.name: Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Balban
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open-access ruin inside Mehrauli Archaeological Park. No ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily, roughly sunrise to sunset.
stops.accessibility: Rough ground and rubble around the ruin; not accessible for wheelchairs.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the shallow dome-less chamber with the true arch: historians call this India's first true arch, and it is hiding in a pile of rubble most people walk past.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back west across the park on the main trail for about 500 metres, following the signs to Rajon Ki Baoli. You will hear the stepwell's parakeets before you see the steps.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Harvinder Chandigarh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
What you are looking at is, frankly, a pile of rubble with a PhD. This was the tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Balban, the iron-fisted Sultan of Delhi who ruled from 1266 to 1287 and held the Sultanate together through Mongol invasions by being, by all accounts, terrifying. He demanded that his courtiers prostrate themselves before him, invented a court etiquette of near-divine grovelling, and kept the Mongols out of Delhi for twenty years. When he died, he was buried here, on what was then the outskirts of his capital.

The tomb itself is a square chamber of rubble masonry, long since collapsed into the brooding ruin in front of you. But walk up to the doorway and look at the arch over it, because architectural historians make pilgrimages to this exact spot. The arch spanning the entrance is a true arch: wedge-shaped stones locked together so each holds the next in place. Every arch you will see later today, from the mosque screens at the Qutub complex to the domes of Hauz Khas, descends from experiments like this one.

Here is the delicious irony. In Balban's own lifetime, Indian masons built with beams and brackets, the trabeate system, and the arch as a structural idea had barely arrived from Central Asia. Balban's tomb, dated to around 1287, contains what is widely called the first true arch in Indo-Islamic architecture. The most feared autocrat of the thirteenth century is remembered less for his terror than for a doorway.

Beside it stands a smaller ruined tomb believed to belong to Khan Shahid, Balban's beloved son and heir, who was killed fighting the Mongols near Multan in 1285. Balban is said never to have recovered from the grief. Stand between the two ruins for a moment: the stern father and the lost son, the arch and the rubble, and the whole Delhi Sultanate in miniature.

stops.name: Rajon Ki Baoli Stepwell
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open-access ASI monument. No ticket; the steps are fenced at the water level for safety.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily, roughly sunrise to sunset.
stops.accessibility: Steep stone steps down four storeys with no railings on the lower flights. Viewable step free from the top rim; do not attempt the steps in the rain.
stops.insiderTip: Walk down to the second landing and turn around: the symmetry of the steps, arches and the mosque at the far end lines up into the single best photograph in the park.
stops.nextStopDirections: Climb back out and take the trail north east for about 400 metres towards the park's northern edge. The domed tomb with the garden plinth ahead is Quli Khan's.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rupeshsarkar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Now for the prettiest hole in the ground in Delhi. A baoli is a stepwell: a deep masonry well with flights of steps descending to the water, so people could walk down to whatever level the water table offered that season. This one was commissioned in 1506 by Daulat Khan, an administrator of the Lodi dynasty, and its name means the masons' stepwell, because the raj mistris, the master masons, are said to have used it. It descends four storeys, each level arcaded with arched niches, and at the far end stands a small mosque with a pointed dome.

Walk down slowly, counting the landings. The geometry does something lovely as you descend: the long stair corridor narrows, the arches stack above you in receding frames, and the temperature drops a good five degrees. In a Delhi summer, which is to say most of the year, this was air conditioning carved in stone. Stepwells were social infrastructure as much as engineering: women gathered here, travellers rested here, and the water served the whole neighbourhood.

Look at the detailing as you go. The walls carry carved bands, the niches once held lamps, and the mosque at the bottom end has finely cut mihrabs. The Archaeological Survey has fenced off the water itself, so admire the green depths from the lowest landing and no further.

A word of honest caution, because the voice in your ear cares about your ankles. The steps are steep, worn smooth by five centuries of feet, and there are no railings on the lower flights. Hold the handrail where one exists, wear shoes with grip, and skip the descent entirely in the monsoon, when the stone turns to soap. The view from the top rim, with the parakeets rattling in the neem trees, is ninety per cent of the pleasure anyway.

stops.name: Quli Khan's Tomb (Metcalfe's Dilkusha)
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open-access ASI monument at the park's northern edge. No ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily, roughly sunrise to sunset.
stops.accessibility: A low plinth with steps; the surrounding lawn is level but the tomb platform is not step free.
stops.insiderTip: Climb the plinth and look north: the Qutub Minar rises over the trees, and the British resident who stole this tomb as a country house picked the view on purpose.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park by the northern path, cross towards Mehrauli and follow the road signs to the Qutub Complex, about 600 metres north. Enter through the main ticket gate; the minar is unmissable from there.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Harvinder Chandigarh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
This handsome domed tomb on its garden plinth has lived at least three lives, and only the first was respectable. It was built in the early 1600s as the tomb of Muhammad Quli Khan, a Mughal noble. Octagonal drum, high dome, arched verandahs on every face: a textbook late-Mughal garden tomb, the kind of building the empire produced the way other states produce paperwork.

Then came the second life, and it is the reason the guides grin. In the 1840s Sir Thomas Metcalfe, the British Resident at the Mughal court, took a fancy to the monuments of Mehrauli and simply moved in. He converted this tomb into his country retreat and renamed it Dilkusha, the heart's delight. He added a verandah, planted gardens, threw parties, and used the rooftop to admire the Qutub Minar, which you can still see from here. The Mughal emperor still nominally ruled Delhi; his would-be overlord was holding dinner parties in a stolen tomb half a mile away. The symbolism was not subtle.

After 1857 the British grew less romantic about living in tombs, and the building drifted back into archaeology. Today the Archaeological Survey keeps it as one of the anchors of the northern park, and the interior holds the graves once again in quiet.

Climb the plinth, circle the verandah, and note the tile traces and plaster medallions inside. Then face north for the view that sold Metcalfe the place: the minar floating over the treetops. You are about to walk to exactly that tower, and the stroll from a tomb-garden to the great minaret is one of the great short walks in Delhi.

stops.name: Qutub Minar
stops.entranceFeeNote: ASI ticketed complex: about ₹40 for Indian visitors and about ₹600 for foreign visitors at last check. Climbing the minar has been closed since 1981. Verify prices at the gate; ASI revises them.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 07:00 to 17:00. Arrive before 09:00 to beat the school groups and the heat.
stops.accessibility: Paved paths around the base with some steps; the tower itself cannot be entered. Wheelchair users get a fine view from the lawns.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the base and look straight up: each of the five storeys has a different surface treatment, because three sultans and one lightning strike each left a signature.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk about 60 metres south east into the mosque courtyard at the foot of the minar. The tall carved stone screen in front of you is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Syed Sajidul Islam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Look up. Keep looking. The Qutub Minar is 73 metres of red sandstone and marble attitude, the tallest brick minaret in the world, and it has been showing off over Delhi for eight hundred years. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, the first Sultan of Delhi, ordered it in 1199 to announce the new order: Islam had arrived in Delhi, it intended to stay, and it could build very, very tall. His successor Iltutmish added three more storeys; a lightning strike in 1368 brought the top down, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the last two in white marble, which is why the tower changes colour near the crown.

Walk slowly around the base and read the tower like a document. The lowest storey carries alternating angular and rounded flutes, carved with Quranic inscriptions in elaborate calligraphy. The balconies, resting on honeycomb muqarnas corbelling, mark where each sultan's contribution ends and the next begins. The iron bands and the Devanagari mason marks remind you that Hindu craftsmen built a Muslim tower, just as they had built the mosque at its feet from temple stone.

Was it a minaret for the call to prayer, or a tower of victory? Scholars still argue, which tells you it worked: eight centuries later we are still discussing Aibak's press release.

Practical notes, because this is the one ticketed stop on the walk. The complex is busy from mid-morning, the lawns offer little shade, and the tower interior has been closed to climbers since a 1981 accident, so enjoy it from the grass. Buy water at the gate, keep your ticket until you exit, and give the tower a full slow circuit: it looks like a different building from every side.

stops.name: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the same Qutub Complex ticket; no separate charge. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Same hours as the Qutub Complex, roughly 07:00 to 17:00 daily.
stops.accessibility: Level courtyard paving with some uneven ancient slabs. The colonnades have low thresholds.
stops.insiderTip: Run your eye along the screen's carvings: behind the Quranic bands you can still spot Hindu bell-and-creeper motifs the masons carved from habit, or from mischief.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk about 50 metres into the middle of the courtyard. The rust-brown pillar standing alone among the columns is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: chopr, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
You are standing in India's first mosque, and it wears its history like scar tissue. The Quwwat-ul-Islam, the Might of Islam, was raised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak starting in 1193, immediately after his conquest of Delhi, on the site of a cluster of Hindu and Jain temples. An inscription on the eastern gateway says as much, bluntly: twenty-seven temples were demolished and their materials reused here. Whether you read that as conquest memorial or as pragmatic recycling, and historians do both, the evidence is in front of you.

Face the great carved screen, added a few years later under Iltutmish. Five enormous corbelled arches rise before you, stitched with Quranic calligraphy and arabesque. Now look closer at the pillars of the colonnade behind it: temple columns, carved with bells, creepers and figures, pressed into service for the new faith, their faces sometimes defaced, sometimes simply left mid-pattern. No two pillars match. The whole courtyard is spolia, beautiful and unsettling in equal measure.

The engineering tells the deeper story. The screen's arches are corbelled, stones stepped inward course by course, because the true arch had not yet entered the Indian mason's toolkit. Remember Balban's little doorway from an hour ago? That experiment, and others like it, is what eventually freed builders from corbelling and made the domes of the later Sultanate possible. This courtyard is the before picture.

Walk the colonnade slowly and count the motifs. The masons who carved creepers and diamonds into an Islamic screen were the same craftsmen who had carved temples a season earlier. Styles do not convert as fast as cities do, and this mosque is the proof.

stops.name: Iron Pillar of Delhi
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the same Qutub Complex ticket; no separate charge. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Same hours as the Qutub Complex, roughly 07:00 to 17:00 daily.
stops.accessibility: Level courtyard, fenced at close range; fully viewable step free.
stops.insiderTip: Read the Sanskrit inscription low on the shaft if the light is kind: it praises King Chandra, and it is the pillar's own birth certificate, sixteen centuries old.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk about 90 metres south past the minar's base to the small sandstone gateway with the dome and carved bands. That is Alai Darwaza.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hridya08, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Seven metres of rust-proof iron, sixteen hundred years old, standing in the middle of a medieval mosque courtyard like a guest who arrived early and never left. That is the Iron Pillar, and metallurgists still write papers about it. The pillar was forged in the early 400s, during the Gupta age, and raised originally somewhere else, most likely in Madhya Pradesh, as a standard to the god Vishnu. A Sanskrit inscription low on the shaft praises a king called Chandra, generally identified as Chandragupta the Second, and records the pillar as his victory standard.

It came to Delhi centuries later, probably dragged here by a Tomar or Chauhan king, and the builders of the mosque simply built around it. Which gives you the strangest layering on this walk: a Hindu imperial standard, inscribed in Sanskrit, standing in the courtyard of India's first mosque, next to a minaret built to celebrate that mosque's religion. Delhi does not do chronological order. It does palimpsest.

Now the famous party trick. The pillar is nearly pure wrought iron, forge-welded, with a high phosphorus content that has grown a protective passive film over the centuries. Sixteen hundred monsoons have left it essentially rust-free, while your garden gate surrenders in six. Modern archaeometallurgy calls it a masterpiece; the inscription on the pillar just calls Chandra's fame what it is.

There used to be a tradition that embracing the pillar with your back to it brought luck, and generations of visitors polished the shaft at hugging height. The fence you see is the Archaeological Survey protecting a world treasure from affection. Photograph it, read the old Devanagari if the light allows, and leave the hugging to history.

stops.name: Alai Darwaza
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the same Qutub Complex ticket; no separate charge. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Same hours as the Qutub Complex, roughly 07:00 to 17:00 daily.
stops.accessibility: A few steps at the doorway; the interior chamber floor is level once inside.
stops.insiderTip: Step inside and look up at the dome: the horseshoe-shaped squinches holding it up are the first true dome built in India, and every Mughal dome after it is the grandchild.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the metro hop, not a walk: the next stop is 5.1 km north — about seventy minutes on foot along busy roads — so do not stroll it. Exit the complex, walk 10 minutes to Qutub Minar metro station (Yellow Line), ride four stops to Hauz Khas, then take an auto or a 15-minute walk east to the Hauz Khas Complex entrance. Allow about 40 minutes door to door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: stevekc, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
End the Qutub complex at its most perfect small building. The Alai Darwaza, the Gate of Alauddin, was built in 1311 by Sultan Alauddin Khalji as the southern entrance to his great extension of the mosque, an extension so ambitious that its unfinished minaret stump still stands north of here, twice the minar's intended girth, abandoned when he died. The gate is what survives of the dream, and it is exquisite.

It is a square chamber of red sandstone inlaid with white marble, capped by a single dome. That dome matters enormously: it rests on squinches, arches thrown across the corners, and it is counted as the first true dome raised in India. Everything you admired at Balban's tomb and the mosque screen was rehearsal; this is opening night. The horseshoe-shaped arches of the doorways, the perforated marble lattices, the carved bands of calligraphy and creeper: Khalji-era craftsmen showing off every technique they owned.

Step inside and look up. The interior dome floats on its squinches with a confidence that still reads as modern, and the light through the lattice screens moves across the stone like water.

Then step back out for the farewell view: the minar, the mosque screen, the pillar and this gateway in one panorama, eight centuries of Sultanate architecture inside a single frame. When you have had your fill, head for the exit. The next leg of this tour is not a stroll but a metro ride, and the directions at this stop spell it out: Hauz Khas, its madrasa and its lake, are waiting four kilometres north.

stops.name: Hauz Khas Madrasa and Tombs
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry to the monument complex; the surrounding Deer Park is also free. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Open daily in daylight hours, roughly 10:00 to 18:00. The lanes of Hauz Khas Village around it stay lively into the evening.
stops.accessibility: Steep steps down from the village entrance and uneven flagstones throughout; not step free, and the lakeside path has drops.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the lake-facing terrace at the far end: the madrasa's domed pavilions line up over the water like a syllabus, and that is where Firoz Shah's own tomb sits among his students' graves.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the lakeside path south along the water for about 100 metres to the main viewpoint. The reservoir spreads out below you: that is the final stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Manan.jain, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Welcome back, via the Yellow Line, to the fourteenth century's idea of a university town. Hauz Khas means the royal reservoir: a great tank dug by Alauddin Khalji around 1296 to water his new city of Siri. Half a century later, Firoz Shah Tughlaq, the most indefatigable builder the Sultanate ever produced, dredged the silted tank back to life and raised a full scholarly campus along its eastern bank: a madrasa, a mosque, pavilions and the tombs of the learned, all in stone, all facing the water.

Enter from the village side and descend towards the lake. The long L-shaped madrasa block runs along the tank's edge: two storeys of small cells and pillared verandahs where students of theology, law and the sciences once lived and studied. Firoz Shah endowed it richly; the chroniclers claim it was the finest seminary of its age, and the Sultan built his own tomb at its southern end, as if to enrol himself permanently among the scholars.

Walk the terrace slowly. The pavilions step down towards the water in a composition of domes, chhatris and broken colonnades that photographers adore and that Delhi's picnickers have adopted as their own. The royal tombs cluster at the far end: Firoz Shah's square domed chamber, severe and plain, surrounded by the graves of his courtiers.

A note on the setting, because it is half the pleasure. The lanes above you, Hauz Khas Village, are Delhi's gallery-and-cafe quarter, all boutiques in medieval masonry. Have chai up there after the monuments. But down here, on the terrace with the water glittering and the parakeets screaming overhead, the fourteenth century is doing just fine without coffee.

stops.name: Hauz Khas Lake and Deer Park
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public park and reservoir. No ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 05:30 to 19:00 for the Deer Park side; confirm locally as timings shift by season.
stops.accessibility: Paved lakeside promenade, mostly level; the best stretch for wheels is the southern embankment.
stops.insiderTip: Stay for the parakeet hour before sunset: thousands of birds come in to roost over the water, and the ruined tombs on the far bank turn gold.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Retrace the lakeside path to the village lanes, where autos wait near the Deer Park gate; Hauz Khas metro station is about 15 minutes on foot.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Ujala.chowdhry, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
End at the water that started it all. The Hauz Khas tank, the Hauz-e-Alai, was dug around 1296 to store monsoon rain for Alauddin Khalji's Siri, the second of Delhi's historic cities. Every Sultanate capital lived or died on water harvesting, and this reservoir, spread below you in a green urban bowl, is the machine that made south Delhi habitable seven hundred years ago. Firoz Shah revived it in the 1350s, the British let it silt, and modern Delhi has restored it as the centrepiece of the Deer Park.

Take the lakeside promenade slowly. To the east the madrasa terraces step down to the shore; to the west the Deer Park spreads in lawns, woodland and enclosures with spotted deer, peacocks and rabbits. The water itself hosts migratory ducks in winter and extremely confident resident geese all year. It is Delhi's strangest successful marriage: a fourteenth-century reservoir, a Mughal-tomb-dotted deer park, and a jogging circuit, all sharing one shoreline.

Find a bench on the southern embankment for the finale. The light goes gold behind the tombs, the parakeets commute overhead in screaming flocks, and the city noise drops to a hum. You began the day with a Sufi poet's tomb in a quiet garden and you end it on the shore of a Sultan's lake.

That is the arc of this walk: eight centuries of Delhi's rulers digging tanks, raising towers and burying their poets, all within a few kilometres of where you are sitting. When you are ready, climb back to the village lanes for dinner. You have earned it, and south Delhi feeds its walkers well.
